reason: Catch blocks echo raw user input ($action, $g_action, $id_doc, $g_id_doc from $_POST/$_GET) directly into the response without any HTML escaping, giving reflected XSS on any PDO error.
The script only echoes static Portuguese strings, uses a parameterized INSERT for the user input, and never reflects $_POST data to the output, so there is no XSS sink.

The shown code merely concatenates theme/package params into a filesystem path and base URL string that is returned, with no HTML output sink or evidence the params are attacker-controlled reflected output.
Classic Zip Slip: filepath.Join(cd, f.Name) is used without verifying the resulting path stays inside cd, so archive entries containing ../ can write files outside the scenario directory.

The ImageMagick command is built by string concatenation with $source/$destination wrapped only in double quotes instead of escapeshellarg, so a filename containing quotes or shell metacharacters injects into the shell command.
Version.php only returns version/metadata strings from git, config and the database with no HTML rendering sink and no attacker-controlled input, so CWE-79 does not apply to this code.

validateProp is a bypassable blocklist sanitizer: startsWith checks on href/src miss vectors like leading whitespace/control characters before javascript:, missing schemes such as data:text/html, and attributes beyond on*, so unsafe markup can pass validation.

User input goes only into a parameterized INSERT and is never echoed back; the only dynamic output is the PDO exception message (an info-leak smell, not attacker-controlled XSS), so the CWE-79 claim is not supported.
execAsync interpolates the uploaded filename (via {filename} in the message) into a shell command string with only double quotes, so a crafted filename with " or $() achieves command injection.
The flagged lines are just imports and a class declaration in an agent workflow file with no SQL construction or database access anywhere, so CWE-89 is inapplicable.
